title: On Developing Leadership Character
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article rejects the historic view of character as fixed, arguing instead that character dimensions such as humility, integrity, and courage can be deliberately developed by practicing the specific behaviors that express them. It walks through an example — building humility by practicing respect, forgiveness, and thoughtfulness — to illustrate how repeated behavior reinforces underlying character traits. The piece ties this framework to the organization's own Admired Leadership catalog of behaviors and closes with a call to action for leaders to start practicing specific behaviors rather than treating character as static.
points: Modern research treats character as dynamic and improvable rather than fixed, contrary to historic assumptions.
Character dimensions are strengthened by deliberately practicing the specific behaviors that express them.
The example of humility shows how practicing respect, forgiveness, and thoughtfulness reinforces that character trait.
Character dimensions like integrity, courage, and accountability are each tethered to identifiable, learnable behaviors.
The article ties this framework to the Admired Leadership behavior catalog as a practical starting point.
quotes: Research over the last few decades has replaced the historic view of character as fixed and immutable to change with a more dynamic view of character dimensions that evolve over time.
Because character is actualized through behaviors and actions, practicing those behaviors can develop the personal qualities we most desire to improve.
The point not to miss is that character is formed and reformed through the practices of everyday life.
Character dimensions such as integrity, courage, temperance, collaboration, and accountability are tethered to specific actions and behaviors that bring them to light.
Great leaders engage in a host of specific behaviors every day. It’s time to start practicing some of them.
